{{Short description|Analytical expression in statistics}}
{{Distinguish|text = [[Laplace's method]], which is based on an essentially identical construction. Whereas [[Laplace's method]] focuses on a limiting behaviour of the integral, Laplace's approximation isn't used in the limit, and considers both integral and integrand. This naming distinction may not be universal}}

{{Bayesian statistics}}

'''Laplace's approximation''' or the '''quadratic approximation''' ('''QUAP''')<ref>{{Cite web |title=quap: Compute quadratic approximate posterior distribution in rmcelreath/rethinking: Statistical Rethinking book package |url=https://rdrr.io/github/rmcelreath/rethinking/man/quap.html |access-date=2026-03-17 |website=rdrr.io |language=en}}</ref> provides an analytical expression for a [[posterior probability distribution]] by fitting a [[Multivariate normal distribution|Gaussian distribution]] with a mean equal to the [[maximum a posteriori|MAP]] solution and [[Precision (statistics)|precision]] equal to the [[Observed information|observed Fisher information]].<ref>{{cite book |first1=Robert E. |last1=Kass |first2=Luke |last2=Tierney |first3=Joseph B. |last3=Kadane |chapter=Laplace’s method in Bayesian analysis |title=Statistical Multiple Integration |series=Contemporary Mathematics |year=1991 |volume=115 |pages=89–100 |isbn=0-8218-5122-5 |doi=10.1090/conm/115/07 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Information Theory, Inference and Learning Algorithms, chapter 27: Laplace's method|first=David J. C.|last=MacKay|url=http://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itprnn/ps/341.342.pdf|year=2003}}</ref> The approximation is justified by the [[Bernstein–von Mises theorem]], which states that, under regularity conditions, the error of the approximation tends to 0 as the number of data points tends to infinity.<ref>{{cite book|last=Hartigan |first=J. A. |authorlink=John A. Hartigan |chapter=Asymptotic Normality of Posterior Distributions |title=Bayes Theory |series=Springer Series in Statistics |location=New York |publisher=Springer |year=1983 |pages=107–118 |isbn= 978-1-4613-8244-7|doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-8242-3_11 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first1=Robert E. |last1=Kass |first2=Luke |last2=Tierney |first3=Joseph B. |last3=Kadane |chapter=The Validity of Posterior Expansions Based on Laplace's Method |pages=473–488 |editor-first=S. |editor-last=Geisser |editor2-first=J. S. |editor2-last=Hodges |editor3-first=S. J. |editor3-last=Press |editor4-first=A. |editor4-last=Zellner |title=Bayesian and Likelihood Methods in Statistics and Econometrics |location= |publisher=Elsevier |year=1990 |isbn=0-444-88376-2 }}</ref>

For example, consider a regression or classification model with data set <math>\{x_n,y_n\}_{n=1,\ldots,N}</math> comprising inputs <math>x</math> and outputs <math>y</math> with (unknown) parameter vector <math>\theta</math> of length <math>D</math>. The [[Likelihood function|likelihood]] is denoted <math>p({\bf y}|{\bf x},\theta)</math> and the parameter [[Prior probability|prior]] <math>p(\theta)</math>. Suppose one wants to approximate the joint density of outputs and parameters <math>p({\bf y},\theta|{\bf x})</math>. Bayes' formula reads:

:<math>
p({\bf y},\theta|{\bf x})\;=\;p({\bf y}|{\bf x},\theta)p(\theta|{\bf x})\;=\;p({\bf y}|{\bf x})p(\theta|{\bf y},{\bf x})\;\simeq\;\tilde q(\theta)\;=\;Zq(\theta).
</math>

The joint is equal to the product of the likelihood and the prior and by [[Bayes' theorem|Bayes' rule]], equal to the product of the [[marginal likelihood]] <math>p({\bf y}|{\bf x})</math> and [[Posterior probability|posterior]] <math>p(\theta|{\bf y},{\bf x})</math>. Seen as a function of <math>\theta</math> the joint is an un-normalised density.

In Laplace's approximation, we approximate the joint by an un-normalised Gaussian <math>\tilde q(\theta)=Zq(\theta)</math>, where we use <math>q</math> to denote approximate density, <math>\tilde q</math> for un-normalised density and <math>Z</math> the normalisation constant of <math>\tilde q</math> (independent of <math>\theta</math>). Since the marginal likelihood <math>p({\bf y}|{\bf x})</math> doesn't depend on the parameter <math>\theta</math> and the posterior <math>p(\theta|{\bf y},{\bf x})</math> normalises over <math>\theta</math> we can immediately identify them with <math>Z</math> and <math>q(\theta)</math> of our approximation, respectively.

Laplace's approximation is

:<math>
p({\bf y},\theta|{\bf x})\;\simeq\;p({\bf y},\hat\theta|{\bf x})\exp\big(-\tfrac{1}{2}(\theta-\hat\theta)^\top S^{-1}(\theta-\hat\theta)\big)\;=\;\tilde q(\theta),
</math>

where we have defined

:<math>\begin{align}
\hat\theta &\;=\; \operatorname{argmax}_\theta \log p({\bf y},\theta|{\bf x}),\\
S^{-1} &\;=\; -\left.\nabla_\theta\nabla_\theta\log p({\bf y},\theta|{\bf x})\right|_{\theta=\hat\theta}, 
\end{align}</math>

where <math>\hat\theta</math> is the location of a mode of the joint target density, also known as the [[maximum a posteriori]] or MAP point and <math>S^{-1}</math> is the <math>D\times D</math> [[Definite matrix|positive definite]] matrix of second derivatives of the negative log joint target density at the mode <math>\theta=\hat\theta</math>. Thus, the Gaussian approximation matches the value and the log-curvature of the un-normalised target density at the mode. The value of <math>\hat\theta</math> is usually found using a [[Gradient descent|gradient based method]].

In summary, we have

:<math>\begin{align}
q(\theta) &\;=\; {\cal N}(\theta|\mu=\hat\theta,\Sigma=S),\\
\log Z &\;=\; \log p({\bf y},\hat\theta|{\bf x}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\log|S| + \tfrac{D}{2}\log(2\pi),
\end{align}</math>

for the approximate posterior over <math>\theta</math> and the approximate log marginal likelihood respectively.

The main weaknesses of Laplace's approximation are that it is symmetric around the mode and that it is very local: the entire approximation is derived from properties at a single point of the target density. Laplace's method is widely used and was pioneered in the context of neural networks by David MacKay,<ref>{{cite journal |last= MacKay |first= David J. C. |date= 1992 |journal= Neural Computation |url= https://authors.library.caltech.edu/13792/1/MACnc92a.pdf |title= Bayesian Interpolation|publisher= MIT Press |volume= 4 |issue= 3 |pages= 415–447 |doi= 10.1162/neco.1992.4.3.415 |s2cid= 1762283 }}</ref> and for [[Gaussian process]]es by Williams and Barber.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Williams |first1= Christopher K. I. |last2= Barber |first2= David |date= 1998 |journal=   IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence|url= https://publications.aston.ac.uk/id/eprint/4491/1/IEEE_transactions_on_pattern_analysis_20%2812%29.pdf |title =Bayesian classification with Gaussian Processes |publisher= IEEE |volume= 20 |issue= 12 |pages= 1342–1351 |doi= 10.1109/34.735807 }}</ref>

== Integrated nested Laplace approximation == 
'''{{vanchor|Integrated nested Laplace approximation}}''' ('''{{vanchor|INLA}}''') is a method for approximate [[Bayesian inference]] based on Laplace's approximation.<ref name="Rue09">{{cite journal |last1=Rue|first1=Håvard|last2=Martino|first2=Sara|last3=Chopin|first3=Nicolas|title=Approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models by using integrated nested Laplace approximations|journal=J. R. Statist. Soc. B|date=2009|volume=71|issue=2|pages=319–392|doi=10.1111/j.1467-9868.2008.00700.x|s2cid=1657669|hdl=2066/75507|hdl-access=free}}</ref> It is designed for a class of models called latent Gaussian models (LGMs), for which it can be a fast and accurate alternative for [[Markov chain Monte Carlo]] methods to compute posterior marginal distributions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Taylor |first1=Benjamin M. |last2=Diggle |first2=Peter J. |date=2014 |title=INLA or MCMC? A tutorial and comparative evaluation for spatial prediction in log-Gaussian Cox processes |journal=Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation |volume=84 |issue=10 |pages=2266–2284 |arxiv=1202.1738 |doi=10.1080/00949655.2013.788653 |s2cid=88511801}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Teng |first1=M. |last2=Nathoo |first2=F. |last3=Johnson |first3=T. D. |date=2017 |title=Bayesian computation for Log-Gaussian Cox processes: a comparative analysis of methods |journal=Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation |volume=87 |issue=11 |pages=2227–2252 |doi=10.1080/00949655.2017.1326117 |pmc=5708893 |pmid=29200537}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Wang |first1=Xiaofeng |title=Bayesian Regression Modeling with INLA |last2=Yue |first2=Yu Ryan |last3=Faraway |first3=Julian J. |date=2018 |publisher=Chapman and Hall/CRC |isbn=9781498727259}}</ref> Due to its relative speed even with large data sets for certain problems and models, INLA has been a popular inference method in applied statistics, in particular [[Spatial analysis|spatial statistics]], [[ecology]], [[seismology]], and [[epidemiology]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Blangiardo |first1=Marta |title=Spatial and Spatio-temporal Bayesian Models with R-INLA |last2=Cameletti |first2=Michela |date=2015 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Ltd |isbn=9781118326558}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Opitz |first1=T. |date=2017 |title=Latent Gaussian modeling and INLA: A review with focus on space-time applications |journal=Journal de la Société Française de Statistique |volume=158 |pages=62–85 |arxiv=1708.02723}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Moraga |first1=Paula |title=Geospatial Health Data: Modeling and Visualization with R-INLA and Shiny |date=2019 |publisher=Chapman and Hall/CRC |isbn=9780367357955}}</ref> It is also possible to combine INLA with a [[finite element method]] solution of a [[stochastic partial differential equation]] to study e.g. spatial point processes and [[Species distribution modelling|species distribution models]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lindgren |first1=Finn |last2=Rue |first2=Håvard |last3=Lindström |first3=Johan |date=2011 |title=An explicit link between Gaussian fields and Gaussian Markov random fields: the stochastic partial differential equation approach |journal=J. R. Statist. Soc. B |volume=73 |issue=4 |pages=423–498 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9868.2011.00777.x |hdl=20.500.11820/1084d335-e5b4-4867-9245-ec9c4f6f4645 |s2cid=120949984 |hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lezama-Ochoa |first1=N. |last2=Grazia Pennino |first2=M. |last3=Hall |first3=M. A. |last4=Lopez |first4=J. |last5=Murua |first5=H. |date=2020 |title=Using a Bayesian modelling approach (INLA-SPDE) to predict the occurrence of the Spinetail Devil Ray (Mobular mobular) |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=18822 |bibcode=2020NatSR..1018822L |doi=10.1038/s41598-020-73879-3  |doi-access=free|pmc=7606447 |pmid=33139744}}</ref> The INLA method is implemented in the R-INLA [[R (programming language)|R]] package.<ref>{{cite web |title=R-INLA Project |url=https://www.r-inla.org |access-date=21 April 2022}}</ref>

=== Latent Gaussian models ===
Let <math>\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,\dots,y_n)</math> denote the response variable (that is, the observations) which belongs to an [[exponential family]], with the mean <math>\mu_i</math> (of <math>y_i</math>) being linked to a [[Generalized linear model#Linear predictor|linear predictor]] <math>\eta_i</math> via an appropriate [[Generalized linear model#Link function|link function]]. The linear predictor can take the form of a (Bayesian) [[additive model]]. All latent effects (the linear predictor, the intercept, coefficients of possible covariates, and so on) are collectively denoted by the vector <math>\boldsymbol{x}</math>. The [[Hyperparameter (Bayesian statistics)|hyperparameters]] of the model are denoted by <math>\boldsymbol{\theta}</math>. As per Bayesian statistics, <math>\boldsymbol{x}</math> and <math>\boldsymbol{\theta}</math> are random variables with prior distributions.

The observations are assumed to be conditionally independent given <math>\boldsymbol{x}</math> and <math>\boldsymbol{\theta}</math>: <math display="block"> \pi(\boldsymbol{y} |\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \prod_{i \in \mathcal{I}}\pi(y_i | \eta_i, \boldsymbol{\theta}), </math> where <math>\mathcal{I}</math> is the set of indices for observed elements of <math>\boldsymbol{y}</math> (some elements may be unobserved, and for these INLA computes a posterior predictive distribution). Note that the linear predictor <math>\boldsymbol{\eta}</math> is part of <math>\boldsymbol{x}</math>.

For the model to be a latent Gaussian model, it is assumed that <math>\boldsymbol{x}|\boldsymbol{\theta}</math> is a Gaussian Markov Random Field (GMRF)<ref name="Rue09" /> (that is, a multivariate Gaussian with additional [[conditional independence]] properties) with probability density <math display="block"> \pi(\boldsymbol{x} | \boldsymbol{\theta}) \propto \left| \boldsymbol{Q_{\theta}} \right|^{1/2} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{x}^T  \boldsymbol{Q_{\theta}} \boldsymbol{x} \right),</math> where <math>\boldsymbol{Q_{\theta}}</math> is a <math>\boldsymbol{\theta}</math>-dependent sparse [[precision matrix]] and <math>\left| \boldsymbol{Q_{\theta}} \right|</math> is its determinant. The precision matrix is sparse due to the GMRF assumption. The prior distribution <math>\pi(\boldsymbol{\theta})</math> for the hyperparameters need not be Gaussian. However, the number of hyperparameters, <math>m=\mathrm{dim}(\boldsymbol{\theta})</math>, is assumed to be small (say, less than 15).

=== Approximate Bayesian inference with INLA ===
In Bayesian inference, one wants to solve for the [[Posterior probability|posterior distribution]] of the latent variables <math>\boldsymbol{x}</math> and <math>\boldsymbol{\theta}</math>. Applying [[Bayes' theorem#Random variables|Bayes' theorem]] <math display="block">
\pi(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y}) = \frac{\pi(\boldsymbol{y} | \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta})\pi(\boldsymbol{x} | \boldsymbol{\theta}) \pi(\boldsymbol{\theta}) }{\pi(\boldsymbol{y})},
</math> the joint posterior distribution of <math>\boldsymbol{x}</math> and <math>\boldsymbol{\theta}</math> is given by <math display="block">
\begin{align}
\pi(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y}) & \propto \pi(\boldsymbol{\theta})\pi(\boldsymbol{x}|\boldsymbol{\theta}) \prod_i \pi(y_i | \eta_i, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \\
& \propto \pi(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \left| \boldsymbol{Q_{\theta}} \right|^{1/2} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{x}^T  \boldsymbol{Q_{\theta}} \boldsymbol{x}  + \sum_i \log \left[\pi(y_i | \eta_i, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \right] \right). 
\end{align}
</math> Obtaining the exact posterior is generally a very difficult problem. In INLA, the main aim is to approximate the posterior marginals <math display="block">
\begin{array}{rcl}
\pi(x_i | \boldsymbol{y}) &=& \int \pi(x_i | \boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{y}) \pi(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y}) d\boldsymbol{\theta} \\
\pi(\theta_j | \boldsymbol{y}) &=& \int \pi(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y}) d \boldsymbol{\theta}_{-j} ,
\end{array}
</math> where <math>\boldsymbol{\theta}_{-j} = \left(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_{j-1}, \theta_{j+1}, \dots, \theta_m \right)</math>.

A key idea of INLA is to construct nested approximations given by <math display="block">
\begin{array}{rcl}
\widetilde{\pi}(x_i | \boldsymbol{y}) &=& \int \widetilde{\pi}(x_i | \boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{y}) \widetilde{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y}) d\boldsymbol{\theta} \\
\widetilde{\pi}(\theta_j | \boldsymbol{y}) &=& \int \widetilde{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y}) d \boldsymbol{\theta}_{-j} ,
\end{array}
</math> where <math>\widetilde{\pi}(\cdot | \cdot)</math> is an approximated posterior density. The approximation to the marginal density <math>\pi(x_i | \boldsymbol{y})</math> is obtained in a nested fashion by first approximating <math>\pi(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y})</math> and <math>\pi(x_i | \boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{y})</math>, and then numerically integrating out <math>\boldsymbol{\theta}</math> as <math display="block">
\begin{align}
\widetilde{\pi}(x_i | \boldsymbol{y}) = \sum_k \widetilde{\pi}\left( x_i | \boldsymbol{\theta}_k, \boldsymbol{y} \right) \times \widetilde{\pi}( \boldsymbol{\theta}_k | \boldsymbol{y}) \times \Delta_k,
\end{align}
</math> where the summation is over the values of <math>\boldsymbol{\theta}</math>, with integration weights given by <math>\Delta_k</math>. The approximation of <math>\pi(\theta_j | \boldsymbol{y})</math> is computed by numerically integrating <math>\boldsymbol{\theta}_{-j}</math> out from <math>\widetilde{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y})</math>.

To get the approximate distribution <math>\widetilde{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y})</math>, one can use the relation <math display="block">
\begin{align}
{\pi}( \boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y}) = \frac{\pi\left(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{y} \right)}{\pi\left(\boldsymbol{x} |  \boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{y} \right) \pi(\boldsymbol{y})},
\end{align}
</math> as the starting point. Then <math>\widetilde{\pi}( \boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y})</math> is obtained at a specific value of the hyperparameters <math>\boldsymbol{\theta} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_k</math> with [[Laplace's approximation]]<ref name="Rue09" /> <math display="block">
\begin{align}
\widetilde{\pi}( \boldsymbol{\theta}_k | \boldsymbol{y}) &\propto \left . \frac{\pi\left(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_k, \boldsymbol{y} \right)}{\widetilde{\pi}_G\left(\boldsymbol{x} |  \boldsymbol{\theta}_k, \boldsymbol{y} \right)} \right \vert_{\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{x}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k)}, \\
& \propto \left . \frac{\pi(\boldsymbol{y} | \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_k)\pi(\boldsymbol{x} | \boldsymbol{\theta}_k) \pi(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k)}{\widetilde{\pi}_G\left(\boldsymbol{x} |  \boldsymbol{\theta}_k, \boldsymbol{y} \right)} \right \vert_{\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{x}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k)},
\end{align}
</math> where <math>\widetilde{\pi}_G\left(\boldsymbol{x} |  \boldsymbol{\theta}_k, \boldsymbol{y} \right)</math> is the [[Laplace's method| Gaussian approximation]] to <math>{\pi}\left(\boldsymbol{x} |  \boldsymbol{\theta}_k, \boldsymbol{y} \right)</math> whose [[Mode (statistics)|mode]] at a given <math>\boldsymbol{\theta}_k</math> is <math>\boldsymbol{x}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k)</math>. The mode can be found numerically for example with the [[Newton's method|Newton-Raphson method]].

The trick in the Laplace approximation above is the fact that the Gaussian approximation is applied on the full conditional of <math>\boldsymbol{x}</math> in the denominator since it is usually close to a Gaussian due to the GMRF property of <math>\boldsymbol{x}</math>. Applying the approximation here improves the accuracy of the method, since the posterior <math>{\pi}( \boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y})</math> itself need not be close to a Gaussian, and so the Gaussian approximation is not directly applied on <math>{\pi}( \boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{y})</math>. The second important property of a GMRF, the sparsity of the precision matrix <math>\boldsymbol{Q}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_k}</math>, is required for efficient computation of <math>\widetilde{\pi}( \boldsymbol{\theta}_k | \boldsymbol{y})</math> for each value <math>{\boldsymbol{\theta}_k}</math>.<ref name="Rue09" />

Obtaining the approximate distribution <math>\widetilde{\pi}\left( x_i | \boldsymbol{\theta}_k, \boldsymbol{y} \right)</math> is more involved, and the INLA method provides three options for this: Gaussian approximation, Laplace approximation, or the simplified Laplace approximation.<ref name="Rue09" /> For the numerical integration to obtain <math>\widetilde{\pi}(x_i | \boldsymbol{y})</math>, also three options are available: grid search, central composite design, or empirical Bayes.<ref name="Rue09" />
